title: The harm of slander
hook: slandering the holy spoils the slanderer's own life (Sukhmani 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sant, the holy one: shelter near good people carries you across. Today the salok's second line takes over the whole ashtpadi.

A group chat, late at night. Someone posts a screenshot of a coworker's message and adds an eye-roll. Within a minute there are six replies. Everyone has a story. Nobody is lying exactly, but by the end the coworker is a joke, and the chat has never been livelier. It feels good, in a sour sort of way. You go to sleep a little buzzed and a little worse. Guru Arjan spends an entire ashtpadi on that buzz, asking the one question the group chat never does: what is this doing to us?
screen: `A SCREENSHOT AND AN EYE-ROLL.` → `SIX REPLIES IN A MINUTE.` → `WHAT IS THIS DOING TO US?`

segments.voice: The thirteenth ashtpadi is built like a drumbeat. Line after line opens with the same three words: sant kai dookhan, through harming the holy, through speaking ill of them. Then each line names a cost. Life is cut short. All peace goes. The mind becomes dirty. Honor is lost. No one comes to help. The list runs stanza after stanza, the opening words returning like a knock on a door. Now look at who pays, in every single line. Not the sant. The good person being slandered never suffers in these stanzas. The losses all fall on the slanderer: their peace, their mind, their standing, their life. That's the surprise, and it turns the group chat upside down. We gossip because it seems to cost the other person something and give us something: a laugh, a bond, a bit of height. Sukhmani says the accounts run the other way. The one being talked about loses very little; the one talking is the one being emptied. Two words to hold. Dookhan: speaking ill, finding fault, doing harm with words. And nindaa, slander, the salok's own word. Even so, the first stanza leaves a door open: if the merciful saint shows mercy, even the slanderer is carried across in the saints' company. And why the holy, especially? Because nearness to the good lifts us, and slander pushes the good away on purpose, and with them the very company that might have carried us across.
screen: `SANT KAI DOOKHAN: A DRUMBEAT.` · `LINE AFTER LINE, A COST.` · `THE SLANDERER ALWAYS PAYS.` · `PUSHING THE GOOD AWAY.` · then, large: `SLANDER HARMS THE SLANDERER.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the mind do what it does, and when it brings up someone who annoys you and starts a little commentary, don't argue with it. Just stop the sentence halfway, like lifting a needle off a record, breathe out, and wait for the next one. You're not forcing kindness yet; you're only learning where the needle is.
Nindaa, slander. Sant kai dookhan, speaking ill of the good: in the thirteenth ashtpadi, line after line, the one who speaks is the one who pays.
Your line: slander harms the slanderer. The one talking is the one who pays. Four hundred eighty-seven days, and counting.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the thirteenth ashtpadi's repeated lines beginning sant kai dookhan, and nindaa, slander, is warned against in many hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib.

chat.says: Everyone vents about that one coworker. What's the harm if she never hears it?
options: Sukhmani says slander costs the one speaking: their peace, their mind and their honor.
The harm comes only if she finds out; words she never hears can't cost anyone.
Gossip is harmless as long as everything we say about her is true and funny.
chat.meaning: In the thirteenth ashtpadi, line after line, the losses fall on the slanderer: peace, a clean mind, honor; never on the one slandered.

Dookhan.meaning: speaking ill, finding fault, harming with words

sant.meaning: a holy person, whose life is soaked in remembering God

ashtpadi.meaning: a section of Sukhmani, eight stanzas long

Guru Arjan.meaning: the fifth Sikh Guru, who wrote Sukhmani

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 13, stanzas 1–3 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279–280)

notes: Paraphrased costs in the sant kai dookhan lines (aarjaa ghatai: life shortened; sukh sabh jaai: peace lost; mat hoi maleen: mind made dirty; sobhaa te heen: honor lost; no one to help): confirm each appears in ashtpadi 13 and their stanza numbers.
Dookhan glossed as speaking ill / harming, related to dookh: confirm the gloss.
Some lines of the ashtpadi also speak of the saint's slanderer in narak, hell; the script paraphrases only the costs listed.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'dookhan, from dookh, pain' (dookhan is usually traced to Sanskrit dushan, defiling or fault-finding, not dukh, pain: a preacher's etymology) and the superlative 'the most common word in Gurbani'; added the end of stanza 1 (sant kirpaal kirpaa je karai, Nanak santsang nindak bhee tarai) so the ashtpadi isn't shown as only threats.
